paragraphs.text: Lesson 14, Crime and Safety
Welcome to Lesson 14 of the Everyday English Speaking Course.
This lesson will teach you vocabulary for talking about crime and safety.
Conversation number one, talking about crime.
Did you hear about the horrible crime in Detroit?
No, what happened?
Some guy kidnapped two teenage girls and kept them locked up for over a year,
raping and beating them constantly.
That's awful!
Those poor girls!
How'd they escape?
A delivery man heard screams coming from inside the house and called the police.
They arrested the guy and rescued the girls.
He's going to be charged with attempted murder since he was threatening to kill them.
I hope he gets sentenced to life in prison.
I don't know what this world's coming to.
Even my own neighborhood isn't safe anymore.
There have been a few break-ins on my street and some of my neighbors have been mugged.
Luckily, it's pretty safe where I live.
The worst that happens is an occasional act of vandalism or trespassing,
usually by some mischievous teenagers.
Did you know I'm related to a convicted criminal?
My uncle was found guilty of insurance fraud five years ago.
Wow, did he have to serve time?
No, he just had to pay a fine of about $50,000.
Crime definitely doesn't pay.
Conversation vocabulary and phrases.
Several crimes are mentioned in this conversation.
Let's learn about the different types of crimes with example sentences of how you can talk about each one.
Violent crime includes crimes that injure or kill someone.
For example, armed robbery.
That's stealing things from a house, business, or bank while using weapons.
The verb is rob, and the person who does this is called a robber.
For example, there was an armed robbery at the jewelry store on Main Street.
The robbers had automatic weapons.
After robbing the store, they escaped in a getaway car.
Assault means physically attacking someone.
The verb is assault, and the person who does it is called the assailant or attacker.
For example, a woman was assaulted while walking home from work.
The assailant beat her up with the baseball bat.
The word murder means to kill someone with intention.
The verb is murder or kill, and the person who does it is called the murderer or killer.
For example, the murderer was an unemployed man in his mid-40s.
He killed his wife in order to get her life insurance money.
Kidnapping refers to taking someone and keeping them prisoner against their will.
The verb is kidnap, and the person who does this is called a kidnapper.
For example, the son of a famous actor was kidnapped last week.
The kidnappers are demanding $10 million in ransom.
Rape and sexual assault refer to having sexual relations with someone when that person doesn't want to.
The verb for this is rape, and the person who does it is called a rapist or attacker.
For example, Laura's testimony helped convict the rapist.
He had raped her multiple times.
And the word mugging refers to stealing from a person in a public place.
The verb is mug, and the person who does this can be called a mugger, thief, or robber.
For example, I was mugged on the subway.
The robber took my cell phone and wallet.
White-color crimes usually involve information or money, but they don't physically injure anyone.
For example, fraud is providing dishonest information so that you can get some advantage.
The verb is commit fraud.
The person who does it is called a fraudster, and there's an adjective, fraudulent.
For example, due to voter fraud, the election results were deemed invalid.
Members of one political party presented fraudulent documents in order to vote multiple times for their favorite candidate.
Identity theft is using someone else's personal information to your advantage.
The verb for this is to commit identity theft, or steal someone's identity.
For example, someone stole my identity and took out a loan in my name.
I should have taken better precautions against identity theft.
Tax evasion means illegally avoiding paying taxes to your country's government.
For example, the CEO of the company was charged with tax evasion.
Bribery means illegally giving someone money in exchange for a special favor.
The verb for this is bribe.
For example, Larry tried to bribe the police officer to let him go without a speeding violation,
but the officer arrested him for attempted bribery.
Blackmail means threatening a person in order to manipulate him or her.
The verb for this is blackmail, and the person is a blackmailer.
For example, the journalist blackmailed the celebrity into giving him an exclusive interview
by threatening to post embarrassing photos online.
Another category of crimes are misdemeanors, which are less serious crimes.
For example, shoplifting, which is stealing something from a store.
The verb is shoplift, and the person is called a shoplifter, or thief.
For example, I shoplifted a few times when I was a teenager.
I got away with it, but nowadays most stores have security cameras to help prevent shoplifting.
Drug possession refers to having illegal drugs, like cocaine, heroin, LSD, etc.
For example, the musician was arrested for drug possession.
Police found a pound of cocaine in his car.
Vandalism is damaging public or private property.
The verb is vandalized, and the person who does it is a vandal.
For example, vandals smashed all the windows in the church, and the new statue in the park was also vandalized.
This town has a real problem with vandalism.
Trespassing means entering another person's property without their permission.
The verb is trespass, and the person is a trespasser.
For example, security guards caught a man suspected of trespassing on government property,
but it turned out he was a legitimate government official, not a trespasser.
Drunk driving, or DUI, means driving under the influence of alcohol.
The verb for this is to drive drunk, or drive under the influence, and the person who does it is called a drunk driver.
For example, a lot of people are arrested for drunk driving on New Year's Eve.
Last year, I saw a drunk driver run three red lights and cause an accident.
The conversation also includes various verbs used to talk about crimes.
To attempt a crime means to try to do it.
For example, he attempted to kidnap the daughter of a politician.
Police are investigating an attempted break-in at the museum.
To be arrested for a crime means to get caught by the police and taken to jail.
For example, two suspects were arrested for assault.
The policeman arrested the shoplifter.
To be accused of a crime means to have someone say that you did it.
For example, the teacher was accused of sexually assaulting one of his students.
The businessman accused his partner of blackmail.
To be charged with a crime means to be officially accused through the legal process.
For example, he'll be charged with attempted murder.
To be suspected of a crime means to have people think that you did it.
For example, Jonas is suspected of embezzlement.
To be acquitted of a crime means to have a judge or jury decide that you're innocent.
For example, Jonas was acquitted because there was no evidence.
To be convicted of a crime means to have a judge or jury decide that you're guilty.
For example, my uncle was convicted of insurance fraud.
To serve time for a crime means to go to prison because you did it.
For example, she served six months for drunk driving.
If you witness a crime, it means you see what happened.
For example, there were no witnesses to the kidnapping.
I witnessed a mugging in Times Square.
And finally, to be a victim of a crime means to have a crime done to you.
For example, many rape victims are afraid to report the crime.
Have you ever been a victim of identity theft?
Finally, let's learn phrases for talking about punishments for crime.
You can say, he received the death penalty.
That means he was executed.
He was sentenced to life in prison.
He was sentenced to five years in jail.
A more informal way to say it is, he got five years.
He had to pay a fine.
He had to do community service.
He got off with the slap on the wrist.
This expression means that the punishment was much lighter than the crime.
Conversation number two, reporting a crime.
Mary is visiting another city and her purse is stolen while she's shopping for souvenirs.
Stop! Thief!
Where's the nearest police station?
On Fifth Avenue, two blocks that way.
How can I help you, ma'am?
My purse was stolen.
When and where did this happen?
Five minutes ago, in front of Joe's souvenir shop on Third Avenue.
Can you describe the robber?
It was a short white guy, probably in his 20s.
He was wearing jeans, a gray t-shirt, and a baseball cap.
Was he armed?
No, I don't think he had a weapon.
He just snatched my purse off my shoulder and ran away.
It all happened so fast.
Can you describe your bag and tell me what was in it?
Documents, cash, personal items?
It's a medium-sized brown leather purse with two short straps.
There was my wallet with about a hundred bucks in cash and two credit cards,
my driver's license, and a Samsung cell phone.
Good thing I left my passport in the safe at the hotel.
Okay, ma'am, I just need you to fill out this form and sign here.
You should call your bank and cancel the credit cards.
I'll let you know if your belongings turn up.
The dialogue begins with Mary shouting, stop thief.
Here are some other phrases you can use in emergencies.
Call the police.
Somebody help me.
Leave me alone.
Go away.
To report the crime, Mary says, my purse was stolen.
Many English learners confuse the words, rob, thief, and steal.
Click on the link in the lesson text for an explanation of the differences between them.
Additional ways to report a crime include, my wallet was stolen, my bag or backpack was stolen,
my passport was stolen, my cell phone was stolen.
I'd like to report a theft.
My car was broken into, my house or apartment was broken into, my office was broken into.
I've been mugged.
I've been raped.
I've been robbed.
The police officer asks Mary to describe the robber.
You can click on the link in the lesson text for a detailed lesson on describing a person's physical characteristics.
Finally, what are some tips for protecting yourself from becoming a victim of a crime?
Keep your valuables in a safe.
Always lock your door.
Install a burglar alarm or a car alarm.
Carry only as much money as you need.
Be aware of your surroundings.
Don't let a stranger into your car or home.
At night, try to walk in well-lit areas.
You've finished lesson 14.
